content.text: 1.2.9 Audio-only (Live)
Learning objectives
Identify live audio-only content, explain what an equivalent alternative for time-based media needs to convey, and plan access during a live audio event. This is a Level AAA criterion.
Making a live audio event available in another form

A live audio-only event has audio with no video or interaction. Examples include an audio stream of a public meeting or a live radio discussion on a website. A person unable to hear the stream needs an alternative that presents equivalent information. Criterion 1.2.9 requires an alternative for time-based media for live audio-only content.

Live text that conveys the speakers' words, identifies speakers when necessary, and includes meaningful sounds can provide an alternative. The specific arrangement depends on the event and technology. A title such as “Meeting in progress” identifies the event but does not convey its discussion, decisions, or questions. A written agenda alone also does not represent information that emerges during the event.

For an event that actually follows a prepared statement or script, providing the accurate text can also be a sufficient approach. Check for deviations: a script that differs materially from what occurred does not convey equivalent information. W3C describes live text as preferable when it can adapt to unscripted changes. Its guidance also explains that the criterion was intended for broadcast audio, not as a blanket requirement for a web app to caption every two-way call irrespective of users' needs.
Prepare, deliver, and verify

Identify every audio source, including callers and audience microphones. Arrange a real-time transcription workflow and provide names, topic vocabulary, and an agenda in advance where possible. Test the feed, the text display, and the way users find it before the event. During the event, check that all speakers and relevant sounds are represented and respond if the feed fails. Review the output for whether it conveys equivalent information; a running text box with missing questions is not enough.

For example, an audio meeting announces a change to a deadline and accepts questions from callers. An effective alternative conveys the new deadline and the questions and answers, with speaker identification as needed. The organizer should test the caller feed rather than transcribing only the host's microphone.
Distinguish related media

Live synchronized audio and video is assessed under 1.2.4 for live captions. Prerecorded audio-only has its own Level A requirements in 1.2.1. If a recording of the live event is later published, evaluate the recording under the applicable prerecorded criteria as well. A transcript created after the event can help later readers, but does not by itself enable access to a live discussion when the information is needed during the event.
Worked example: a public meeting

A streamed public meeting includes a chair and telephone callers. The chair announces that the closing date has moved from Friday to Monday. A caller asks whether existing applications remain valid, and the chair answers yes. An alternative that shows only the prepared agenda misses both the new deadline and the answer, which are the actual information participants need.

A real-time text alternative can represent the announcement, the caller's question and the answer in sequence, identifying speakers when needed. Before the meeting, test the telephone feed and provide the transcription team with names and topic vocabulary. During the meeting, monitor the output for missing callers or a stopped feed. Provide a clear way to reach the live text and a method for reporting problems.
Evaluate the actual event

Compare the text with the audio for a sample period, and review whether the workflow handles changes of speaker, meaningful sounds, and questions from all sources. Automatic transcription may confuse names or miss overlapping speech; the team should evaluate the actual output and address problems rather than assuming that automation guarantees equivalence. If the event is recorded and later published, review the saved version under the applicable prerecorded audio-only requirements. Preserve the complete information and make the alternative easy to find.
Compare a prepared statement with an unscripted event

A spokesperson reads a prepared announcement exactly as written. A linked transcript of that statement may provide an equivalent alternative, as W3C's sufficient techniques explain. The event team should still verify that the speaker follows the text. If the spokesperson adds an unplanned correction or responds to questions, the prepared statement no longer contains all the information conveyed by the event. A real-time text workflow can represent those additions as they happen.

Contrast this with a live public forum where multiple callers speak and decisions evolve during discussion. An agenda or an anticipated list of questions is not an equivalent transcript. Route every relevant microphone and caller feed to the transcription workflow, identify speakers where it matters, and make the live alternative discoverable. If the transcript omits a caller's question, the answer alone may be impossible to understand.

This criterion addresses content, and W3C's Understanding guidance explains its intended focus on audio broadcasts. It does not impose a blanket obligation on a web application to caption every two-person audio call regardless of user needs. Assess the actual content and the responsibilities of its provider or host. Regardless of the implementation, compare the delivered alternative with the information in the audio and correct substantive omissions.
Required lesson activity

Plan a text alternative for a live audio-only discussion involving a host and callers. List the audio feeds, preparation material, display location, and checks for completeness. Write a sample excerpt that identifies a caller, a question, and the host's answer.
